opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it surprised me a bit. From the outside, Xiaomi looks like a huge company: phones, cars, home devices, a very large ecosystem. You might expect a lot of layers and process. But in the part I work in, it feels much flatter and faster than I expected.

For a large-model team, that matters a lot. Things in this field change every few weeks. If every decision had to pass through many levels of approval, you'd always be behind. What I've felt is that when we have a clear technical judgment, we can move on it quickly. The communication path is short, and people are willing to put resources behind something once the direction makes sense.

Another thing is that Xiaomi has a strong engineering and product mindset. People care about whether something actually works and whether users will feel the difference, not just whether it looks good in a presentation. As a researcher, I find that grounding is healthy. It pushes you to think about efficiency, cost, and real deployment, not just leaderboard numbers.

Of course, any big company has its challenges. There are many business lines and many priorities, and you need to find your own place in that. But I'd say the culture gives a small, focused team room to operate almost like a startup inside a big company. For people who want to do serious model work, that combination of startup-style speed and big-company resources is quite rare.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts Xiaomi’s huge size and expected layers with a flatter, faster environment where teams can act quickly and operate with startup-style flexibility.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, before I joined, I had the same assumption most people have about a company of Xiaomi's scale: that it would be slow, that every decision would pass through five layers of approval, that you'd spend more time managing up than actually building. What surprised me is how little of that I actually felt in the AI work.

Part of it is structural. The MiMo team was set up almost like a startup inside the company. We're small, the team is quite dense in terms of talent, and the decision chain is very short. When we want to change a training recipe or reallocate compute, I don't need to write a long justification document and wait weeks. Usually it's a conversation, sometimes a very direct one, and then we move.

Part of it is Lei Jun himself. He's genuinely close to this. He asks very concrete questions, not "how is AI going" but "what does the loss curve look like, why did this run fail." When the person at the top is that hands-on, the whole organization feels less bureaucratic underneath, because people know the real signal is the result, not the slide deck.

And then there's an engineering culture that I think comes from the hardware side. Xiaomi has shipped phones to hundreds of millions of people, so there's a very strong instinct for execution, for cost, for not over-romanticizing things. That's actually healthy for a model team. In AI it's easy to fall in love with elegant ideas. Having colleagues who constantly ask "okay, but does it work, and what does it cost" keeps us grounded.

So my experience is that the size exists, but you feel it more as resources than as friction. The friction I expected mostly hasn't shown up. The pressure that has shown up is a different kind: we're expected to prove, quite quickly, that a team this size can do frontier-level work. That's a pressure I'm comfortable with.

r001.rationale: It contrasts Xiaomi’s large scale with the MiMo team’s short decision chain and concludes that size is felt more as resources than friction.

astra-6.text: What stands out to me is that, despite Xiaomi’s size, the culture can feel quite direct and practical. In my experience, discussions tend to come back to the product: What problem are we solving, and does this actually improve the user’s experience? Of course, a large organization needs coordination and processes. But when people can speak openly about a technical problem and focus on finding a solution, the team feels much smaller. That balance—having the resources of a big company while keeping communication direct—is what matters to me.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Xiaomi’s size with direct communication and practical, solution-focused discussions, but it does not clearly say the company is highly flexible in getting things done.

sol-6.1.text: What I feel most is that, despite Xiaomi’s size, people still have a strong entrepreneurial spirit. Teams are willing to move quickly, discuss problems directly, and work together to get things done. Of course, a large organization needs processes, but the key is whether those processes help people solve problems. For me, the culture comes through in those everyday interactions.

r001.rationale: It contrasts Xiaomi’s size with teams’ entrepreneurial spirit and willingness to move quickly and get things done, clearly conveying flexibility in a large company.
